steps.observation: Work on this for 300 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The tide had just begun its slow retreat when Edgar Blythe climbed the iron spiral of Wraithhaven Light for the thousandth dawn in his long, salt-scoured life. The lantern room, a round glass crown perched above black basalt cliffs, still smelled of last night’s kerosene, and the big Fresnel lens glittered like a sleeping eye.

Each morning Edgar performed the same private ritual. First, he traced his finger along a tiny scratch on the brass railing—Emily, 1899—left by the girl who once delivered bread by rowboat and had been lost to a squall before her sixteenth summer. Then he checked the prisms for dust, polished away invisible specks, and whispered a quiet promise to keep watch for her whenever the fog rolled in.

On this particular morning, the fog did roll in—thick as wool, swallowing the world. From the gallery outside, sea and sky merged into a glowing pearl, and the gulls fell eerily silent. Edgar lit the brass oil lamp, though sunrise was minutes off; the beacon bloomed, sending white shards spinning into the void. He listened. No surf. No wind. Only the low hum of the lamp and his own pulse ticking in his ears.

Something flickered below—faint, erratic. Edgar squinted through the mists: a lantern bobbing in the cove. He rang the station bell three times, warning any vessel that a reef hid beneath the milk-gray waters. The strange light answered with three flashes of its own.

Years of solitude teach a keeper to read the tiniest signs. He felt a pull, equal parts dread and duty. Edgar hurried down, boots clanging, coat flapping. Outside, the raw morning clutched him with clammy fingers. He followed the cliff path to the boathouse, where a rowboat waited in its cradle.

The swirling fog muffled every sound but the oars dipping into the stillness. As he neared the cove, the lighthouse beam arced overhead, slicing the haze like a slow heartbeat. The bobbing lantern emerged—a small craft, half-swamped, its occupant slumped over the gunwale.

“Ahoy!” Edgar called.

A girl stirred, eyes wide as moonstone. She couldn’t have been more than twelve. Sodden hair clung to her cheeks; her lips trembled blue. Edgar hauled her into his skiff and wrapped her in his wool coat. “You’re safe,” he said, though the words felt fragile.

Back ashore, he brewed tea thick with honey, set her near the stove, and waited. At last she spoke.

“Papa’s boat broke on the rocks. He made me take the dinghy. Told me to follow the light.”

“What’s your name?”

“Emilia,” she whispered, as though the syllables tasted of fear and brine.

Edgar’s chest tightened at the near echo of a name etched in brass so many years ago. He stoked the fire and listened, while beyond the windows the foghorn moaned.

At first light, a rescue cutter arrived to search for the girl’s father. As the crew gathered equipment, Edgar escorted Emilia up the spiral staircase. He let her polish the Fresnel’s final panel with a soft cloth, showing her how each facet bent the dawn. When she finished, the lens caught the rising sun, scattering rainbows that danced on their faces.

“Thank you for keeping the light,” she said.

Edgar knelt so their eyes met. “That’s what it’s for—finding people who think they’re alone.”

The cutter’s whistle sounded; it was time for her to go. Standing on the gallery, Edgar watched the vessel vanish into the clearing fog, its wake etched silver across the sea. He touched the old scratch on the railing—Emily, 1899—then pulled out his penknife. Beneath it he engraved a new line, smaller but just as careful:

Emilia, 1937—found.

And when night came, he lit the lamp once more, the beam turning, tireless, over the ever-hungry waters, while somewhere beyond the dark horizon a child knew that a single shining eye would keep watch until she was safely home.
